cards.title: Fu Wen (付稳)
cards.sub: 2017 · technical lead, Weibo hybrid-cloud DCP project
cards.prompt: Weibo's hybrid-cloud lead stated DCP's goal as one capability, a single number. What was it — and which quantity does hitting that number leave completely untouched?
cards.body: Not a feed architect — a capacity engineer. Fu Wen led Weibo's hybrid-cloud DCP project and gave its goal as one capability: finish scaling 1,000 nodes inside ten minutes. That buys parallelism. It buys nothing against the size of the job, which one author's follower count fixes before a single machine boots.
cards.answer: Scaling out 1,000 nodes within ten minutes. It raises how fast work can be absorbed; it does not reduce how much work exists, because one post is one write per follower no matter how many workers are running.

cards.title: Lu Han introduces his girlfriend
cards.prompt: One sentence posted at noon on a Sunday took Weibo out. Who posted it, how long was the platform unusable, and which direction was the load running — out to followers, or in?
cards.body: Lu Han introduced the actress Guan Xiaotong in one line, translated: "Hi everyone, I want to introduce my girlfriend @GuanXiaoTong to you." So many fans commented that the platform was inaccessible for two hours. The load ran inward, converging on one post — not outward into follower timelines.
cards.answer: Lu Han, 8 October 2017; inaccessible for two hours, with SCMP reporting full server function around 4pm. Inward: interaction converging on a single post, not fanout of that post to followers. Same follower count, other end of the pipe.

cards.title: "Follow Whom? Chinese Users Have Different Choice"
cards.sub: Chen, Liu, Wang & Gu · arXiv:1212.0167 · December 2012
cards.prompt: Which open measurement of Weibo's follow graph can you read today, how big was the data set, and what did it find that stops you copying a US fanout threshold?
cards.body: An arXiv paper (cs.SI) built on 80.8 million Sina Weibo profiles and 7.2 billion follow relations, compared against a Twitter dataset. Its finding: Weibo's following preference is more concentrated and hierarchical than Twitter's — people follow upward. So the tail you size fanout for is not Twitter's tail.
cards.answer: Chen, Liu, Wang and Gu, arXiv:1212.0167, December 2012 — 80.8 million profiles and 7.2 billion relations. Weibo's following preference is more concentrated and hierarchical than Twitter's, so the shape of the tail, and therefore the push/pull threshold, does not transfer.

cards.title: DCP, the ten-minute fleet
cards.sub: 2016 Spring Festival · Weibo with Alibaba Cloud
cards.prompt: Weibo could stand up a thousand machines in ten minutes and had proved it at a national peak. Say why that leaves a push/pull threshold exactly as load-bearing as before.
cards.body: At the 2016 Spring Festival, Weibo and Alibaba Cloud created more than 1,000 ECS instances hours before the peak, average scale-out under ten minutes. Elasticity divides a job across more workers. The job's size is a number in someone else's account. Faster is not smaller.
cards.answer: More workers raise aggregate throughput without reducing the total work one tap creates — still one write per follower. Rented capacity shortens the queue, never the follower list, so the design must still refuse the fanout above some follower count.
